traces.answer:
Criticizing a VP of Sales who cannot do better is counterproductive
https://t.co/8cYlOq0HkV

As I’ve shared many times on SaaStr over the years, hiring a “wrong fit” VPS can end up costing you almost as much as if you’d never hired anyone at all.  If they don’t work out, and you just let things slide … it’s hard to get back to where you were before.
But what happens when your new VPS does OK — for a while? But then doesn’t really grow your revenue anymore?
Should you criticize him or her, point fingers, make demands? Or will that hurt morale even further? I.e., can you ever move forward past this stage?
I’m not sure there’s a simple answer. Let me share my learnings here:
First, some bad VPs of Sales will take advantage of time. They’ll promise to hire their top reps, but won’t actually do so. So yes, they’ll look good initially — at first. Then later, they’ll have zero people left underperforming. Which often looks even worse than before. Don’t play these games. It always ends badly. Instead, find someone else to replace any failing sales execs asap. Second, sometimes it’s best to just agree to disagree on performance issues. Sometimes, a VP of Sales will push back on how many leads she needs per rep, or how big an ACV she can close, etc. There’s nothing wrong with pushing back against an unrealistic goal set by management. But it also doesn’t help if you argue too much here. Instead, just agree on goals that are achievable given the current state of the company. Third, don’t expect miracles from a mediocre VP of Sales.

traces.answer: So I've talked on SaaStr for years now about hiring a great VP of Sales. How to hire her. What mistakes you make when you don't find a good one. But there were two points that we didn't dig into too much. And so let me just quickly summarize those today because they're super important if you haven't figured this out yet. Number one, don't criticize your VPS. Don't tear him apart over the internet. If she can't get it done, then move on. But don't criticize her publicly. Because that is almost always counterproductive. It undermines their confidence. It undermines morale. In fact, most VPs will quit after public criticism. So instead, what you need to do is backfill him. Help him. And if you have to go another month, you'll survive. Your revenue will still grow. It won't kill you. But tearing someone down doesn't help anyone. Number two, folks want to know whether or not a great VP of Sales needs to bring in all these reps under them. Can they really do it alone? Well, yes and no. Yes, if it's early stage, maybe start off with just one rep yourself. Maybe even zero. If it's later stage, well then probably you need three to four reps in the first week or two. And a VP of Sales that wants to work themselves up from nothing, well, they might be able to do that. They might want to put in the effort. But that's rare. It's very hard to do it without any experience. And ultimately, if you want to scale faster than 10x, you're going to need to hire ahead of time. We've also learned since Covid that folks aren't as interested in working remotely anymore. Many VPs of Sales, many CROs want to manage reps in the office. They want to fly around.
